samasa.sense: she who is the ground on which the world rests
samasa.alt: Compounds in -भूत are also treated as a supsupā compound (‘any case with any case’); the sense, ‘being the support’, is the same.

samasa.literal: by the form of the earth

samasa.sense: existing as (the waters); the genitive अपाम् outside the compound depends on its first member स्वरूप

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (its first member अलङ्घ्य is a nañ tatpuruṣa: न लङ्घ्यम्)
samasa.literal: whose might is not to be overstepped

morph.note: Present ātmanepada of आ + √प्यै (प्याय-): ‘swells, is filled, thrives’. It is intransitive, not a passive; त्वया names the one through whom the world is nourished.
Genitive plural of अप् ‘water’, a feminine noun used only in the plural (nom. आपः, instr. अद्भिः, gen. अपाम्).
लङ्घ्य is a gerundive (√लङ्घ् ‘to leap over’ + -ya): ‘to be overstepped’; with the negative अ-, ‘not to be overstepped’, i.e. irresistible.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अलङ्घ्यवीर्ये, त्वम् एका जगतः आधारभूता (असि), यतः महीस्वरूपेण स्थिता असि। अपां स्वरूपस्थितया त्वया एतत् कृत्स्नम् आप्यायते।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the first states that she alone is the support of the world and gives the reason in a यतः clause; the second, with the intransitive verb आप्यायते, says the whole world is nourished through her as water. The vocative stands at the end.
mantras.lit: You alone are the support of the world, since you abide in the form of the earth. By you, abiding in the form of the waters, this whole (world) is nourished, O you whose might cannot be overcome.
mantras.tr: You alone are the ground on which the world rests, for you abide as the earth. And as the waters you nourish this whole world, O Goddess of invincible power.
mantras.tr_note: The tr turns ‘by you … this whole is nourished’ into an active sentence (‘you nourish’); the vocative is rendered ‘O Goddess of invincible power’.

comm.t: The gods name two of the elements as her forms. As earth she holds the world up; as water she makes it swell and thrive. The word यतः makes the first line a reason: she is the world’s support because she is the earth.

The verse continues the teaching of Brahmā’s hymn, that the Goddess is not only the power behind the world but its very substance (1.76: त्वयैतत्पाल्यते, ‘by you this is protected’). Earth and water are named because they are the ground and the nourishment of life; the tradition reads them as standing for all the elements.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names मही (718), ‘the earth’, and सर्वाधारा (659), ‘the support of all’. The agreement is in shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.
A modern reading: the ground under one’s feet and the water one drinks are named here as the Goddess herself. Reverence begins with what is most ordinary and most needed.

samasa.sense: the one through whom beings are set free

morph.note: मोहित is the past participle of the causative मोहयति ‘causes to be bewildered’: the world ‘has been bewildered’ — by her, as the previous line implies. Compare 1.55, तया सम्मोह्यते जगत्.
A tatpuruṣa keeps the gender of its last member: हेतु is masculine, so ‘you (f.) are the cause’ is त्वं … मुक्तिहेतुः, as in 4.9 (या मुक्तिहेतुः).
Taddhita: विष्णु + aṇ with vṛddhi of the first syllable (वैष्णव) and feminine -ī: ‘belonging to Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu’s’.

mantras.anvaya: त्वम् अनन्तवीर्या वैष्णवी शक्तिः (असि)। (त्वं) विश्वस्य बीजं परमा माया असि। (हे) देवि, एतत् समस्तं (त्वया) सम्मोहितम्। त्वं वै प्रसन्ना (सती) भुवि मुक्तिहेतुः (भवसि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four predications about the Goddess: Viṣṇu’s power, the seed of the world, the supreme Māyā (verb असि), and, when gracious, the cause of liberation. Between them stands the effect of her Māyā: the whole world is bewildered.
mantras.lit: You are the power of Viṣṇu, of boundless might; you are the seed of the universe, the supreme Māyā. All this, O Goddess, is held in delusion; you indeed, when pleased, are the cause of liberation on earth.
mantras.tr: You are Viṣṇu’s own power, boundless in might, the seed of the universe, the supreme Māyā. By you, O Goddess, this whole world is held in enchantment; and you, when you are gracious, are the cause of liberation on earth.
mantras.tr_note: ‘By you’ in the third sentence is supplied: the participle सम्मोहितम् implies an agent, and the verse has just named her as Māyā.

comm.t: The verse holds both sides of the Goddess together: as Māyā she keeps the whole world bewildered, and when she is pleased she is the cause of release. Binding and freeing come from the same power.

This is the teaching of the first carita repeated in the gods’ mouths: Mahāmāyā, Hari’s power, bewilders the world (1.55), and when gracious (प्रसन्ना) she becomes the cause of liberation (1.57). ‘Vaiṣṇavī śakti’ recalls the name Viṣṇumāyā under which the gods praised her in chapter 5 (5.14–16).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names वैष्णवी (892), विष्णुमाया (339), महामाया (215) and मुक्तिदा (736), ‘giver of liberation’. The names belong to a shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.
A modern reading: what clouds the mind and what clears it are not two rival forces here. The same reality appears as confusion while it is resisted and as freedom once it is met with devotion.

sandhi.note: Visarga before t becomes s. Before s the visarga is kept (विद्याः समस्ताः, स्त्रियः समस्ताः, समस्ताः सकलाः, स्तुतिः स्तव्यपरा).
-āḥ before a voiced sound becomes -ā (the y from the visarga is dropped before a consonant).
ā + e → ai. The same in अम्बयैतत् (अम्बया + एतत्).

sandhi.rule: मोऽनुस्वारः (8.3.23) applies only before a consonant; वृद्धिरेचि (6.1.88)
sandhi.note: The m of पूरितम् is kept before the vowel and written with it; then ā + e → ai.
In the compound the feminine परा takes the masculine stem form पर (a karmadhāraya), and a + u → o.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (पर at the end of a compound: ‘having … as its chief concern’)
samasa.literal: having what is to be praised as its chief concern
samasa.sense: speech whose whole business is something worth praising — the definition of a hymn
samasa.alt: Also read as a pañcamī tatpuruṣa, स्तव्येभ्यः परा, ‘beyond the things that can be praised’, and referred to the Goddess (‘you who are beyond the praiseworthy’). But the word is nominative and agrees with स्तुतिः, not with the genitive ते; the bahuvrīhi keeps the grammar of the line.
Also read as परा उक्तिः in the sense of ‘the supreme Word’ (the Goddess as speech itself); again the agreement with स्तुतिः favours ‘exalted utterance’.

morph.note: Nominative plural of स्त्री: the ī becomes iy before a vowel ending (स्त्रि-य्-अः) instead of y, an irregularity of this word.
Locative plural of जगत्: the ending -su is added directly to the stem in t.
स्तव्य is a gerundive of √स्तु with -ya (yat): the root vowel takes guṇa (स्तो-) and o becomes av before the y (स्तव्य), ‘to be praised’.
Participle of the causative stem पूरय- (√पॄ ‘fill’) with -ita: ‘made full, filled’. Its agent is त्वया एकया … अम्बया, ‘by you alone, the Mother’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, समस्ताः विद्याः तव भेदाः (सन्ति); जगत्सु समस्ताः सकलाः स्त्रियः (तव भेदाः)। त्वया एकया अम्बया एतत् पूरितम्। ते का स्तुतिः (स्यात्)? (स्तुतिः हि) स्तव्यपरा परोक्तिः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two nominal sentences (all knowledge, all women are her forms); a passive one (the world is filled by her alone); then a question and, in apposition, what praise is: the last two nominatives define स्तुतिः.
mantras.lit: All branches of knowledge, O Goddess, are your distinct forms; all women in the worlds, every one of them. By you, the one Mother, this (world) is filled. What praise is there of you — (praise being) an exalted utterance directed to what is to be praised?
mantras.tr: Every branch of knowledge, O Goddess, is a form of you, and so is every woman in all the worlds. You alone, the Mother, fill this whole world. What praise can there be of you? Praise is lofty speech about something to be praised.
mantras.tr_note: The last pāda is read as a definition of praise: praise speaks of something as its object, and the verse has just said there is nothing she does not fill. The other reading (‘you who are beyond the praiseworthy, the supreme Word’) is given under Samāsa and in the flags.

comm.t: Every form of knowledge and every woman in every world are named as her own forms, and the whole world is filled by her alone. The verse then asks what praise could be offered to such a one: praise speaks of an object, and there is nothing outside her to speak of.

The Śākta tradition has drawn from this verse its teaching that every woman is to be honoured as a form of the Goddess. The ‘branches of knowledge’ are traditionally understood as all the sciences, sacred and secular. The doubt about praise is a classic theme of hymns: the hymn goes on praising while confessing that praise cannot reach her (compare 4.4 and 4.6, and the close of Brahmā’s hymn, 1.83–85: कस्त्वां स्तोतुमिहेश्वरः).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names विद्या (549) and विद्याऽविद्यास्वरूपिणी (402), ‘whose form is both knowledge and ignorance’. The idea is shared Śākta thought; the two texts are separate works.
A modern reading: the verse places the sacred in the women one actually meets and in every honest form of learning. Its reverence is meant to be practised in ordinary life, not kept for the shrine.

flags.uncertain: The last pāda, स्तव्यपरा परोक्तिः, is read in two ways: as a definition of praise in apposition to स्तुतिः (‘an exalted utterance directed to what is to be praised’), followed here because both words are nominative like स्तुतिः; or as epithets of the Goddess (‘beyond the praiseworthy, the supreme Word’), which needs त्वम् to be understood. Both readings are traditional in translation; the point of the verse — no praise can match her — is the same.
